Instructions to fit ALL machines - I have to update this because I got the instructions for making this work with my K Classic. When I first tried to use it, I thought it didn't fit and couldn't figure out why. So here you go:

What you have to do for this to fit the K Classic and some others is to REMOVE the K-Cup holder that is already in the brewer. It's not hard to remove; I just never thought it came out! LOL See my photo.

Once you remove that piece from the machine, then, you can replace it with the Universal device. (Also, remember that to detach that universal adaptor, it helps to remove the label/sticker that attaches it to the top half. I could not get the adaptor off for a minute until I saw that it was taped to the other piece! Duh.)

The thing here is that this reusable filter is not used exactly like the off-market ones; this one is made to REPLACEthat part of the machine where we normally sit a filled K-cup.

I felt like an idiot until I realized this is a huge missing piece of info in the package instructions. I had already packed my up and arranged for a refund - and then ordered another set. I sure hope I can cancel the other set! Ugh!!!

The other thing I had to figure out is that when I do want to use a store-bought K-cup - which I sometimes do if they are on sale - then I need to put the old K-cup part back in (the one I removed and replaced with the universal one) so that the store-bought K-cup fits again. It's not hard to swap them out after you do it once.

I really hope this helps the other people who didn't think this fit their machine. I have the Classic K 55 machine, by the way.

Now I have to tell you that this universal cup does work 110% better than any other reusable cup that I have used. So glad that it fit.

Terrible Design, hard to use, easy to make a mess - I have a K-Supreme Coffee Maker which is a masterfully designed machine. But the Keurig designers must have been drunk when they designed this reusable K-Cup. First, you have to remove the standard basket from your machine. That's not too hard (putting it back is a different story), but it is a two handed job, and don't forget to do it or you will puncture your K-Cup. Then you have to take the K-cup apart (3 pieces) and fill it with just the right amount of coffee, if it's not enough it will taste like dish water, but if you go past the dark fill line on the dark inside of the basket you will make a mess. (anyone over 50 knows that seeing dark marks on a dark background in a dark kitchen before you've had your first coffee is a bad design). Then you have to put it back together, first lining up the cap, then fitting the inner basket into the outer basket and getting the tab just right. Then you have to insert the black basket into the black hole in your machine and get both the black tab and the arrow aligned just right. If not, you will make a huge mess and fill both your machine and coffee mug with wet coffee grounds. Not the way I like to start my day. But beware that putting the standard basket back in is just as tricky and fraught with potential mess.

I've gone back to my drip coffee maker. It's hard to screw that up.

No more loud dogs or kids!!! - Oh man! So i bought this and let it sit in the box for about a month until i finally found the energy and time to replace it and wow what a differece. My old one was flimsy and did not have any real type of seal, just a very loose hanging flap inside that was meant to keep out backdrafts but failed miserably. It also even let in sunlight somehow? So i ended up ripping out the old one and preparing my house for the new one. The way i did it was with aviation snips, channel locks, and a hammer and chisel. My house is made of brick so i just used the hammer and chisel to clean off the old sealant that was used. Just angle the chisel at a sharp angle to avoid damaging the brick and with a few light taps the sealant was scraped right off. I used tuff stuff spray insulation foam to seal up big gaps which worked out great. The sprayed some more to be sure any remaining gaps are filled. I put in plastic anchors to hold in the 4 screws for this thing as well as sealant to make it air and water tight. A nice bead of sealant on the backside and a bead of sealant on the edge once it was screwed down tight. Then on the inside i used foil tape to seal it all up against the drywall. I took the opportunity to seal up the fan area on the range hood to help it direct more air outside. I also used 1/4" wide strips of weather stripping around the exhaust side of the range hood to make sure it has an airtight seal. Now that it's all done. My house is sooooooooooo much quieter! No more banging of the flimsy flap from the old vent, i can no longer hear the loud wild neighbor kids, i can no longer hear their small yappy dog and now when we cook, the smell of the food no longer permeates the entire house. I highly recommend taking the extra steps to make sure it's air tight on the range hood side. I have a good feeling that this one will last a long time.

Install tips - The pump is pretty straight forward to install. I suggest tipping the washer forward onto a pad for easy access to the pump and protection of the washer. The only difficult bit is installing the fuse. The directions are a little vague on this (and there are two options on where to install the fuse depending on the exact model of washer you have). The fuse is added into the console (the part on the top of the washer that has the key-pad on it). To get access to the area where you need to add the fuse, you need to 1) remove the lid of the washer (swing it straight up into the position it would be when you add clothes and then pull the lid straight up) and 2) remove two screws from the back of the console.
Then the scary bit - you will need to find the correct wire based on the directions (make sure you are following the correct directions for your model!) and then cut the wire and strip the ends. The fuse holder has a single red wire that you will need to cut in two (and strip the ends). Then twist the wires together and crimp with the included connectors. You will need a wire stripper and crimper in addition to a common Phillips head screwdriver. Not hard to do if you have done light home repair jobs before.

In order for the drawers to be tall enough to accommodate regular size dishes, they have to make holder of the dishes very low, which is too close to the spinning drawer. If something, such as the tip of a spoon or even the corner of the utensil holder, dips a little low, the sprayer would not spin properly and you'd end up with a whole drawer of dirty dishes after an 1:30 hour wash. But you can't always test the spinner, since once the dish drawer is full, there is no room to get your hand through the dishes to test the sprayer. And the spaces in the dish-holder are large, so it is easy for something to dip low and block the sprayer. Sometimes I have a half-washed drawer of dishes, sometimes the whole drawer has to be rewashed. After every wash, I have to inspect the dishes one by one to make sure they are cleaned.

Many of the taller dishes will not fit in the drawer. Also, each drawer does not hold that many dishes. If I have a mug on one side, there will not be enough room for a large and small plate to fit side by side. If you are looking for a dishwasher, I recommend the Kitchenaid regular size dishwasher.
